idiom_name: = delete on the copy constructor and copy assignment operator
implementation_notes: Since C++11 the mixin is usually unnecessary: declare `Socket(const Socket&) = delete;` and `Socket& operator=(const Socket&) = delete;` inside the class and every copy is a compile error whose diagnostic names the deleted function. The base-class form survives as an intent anchor (`boost::noncopyable`, a project-local `NonCopyable`, or the template form from More C++ Idioms) and as the only option for pre-C++11 toolchains, where the copy operations were declared private and left undefined. Declaring the copy operations also suppresses the implicit move operations, so a move-only type must add defaulted moves.
pitfalls: Deleting the copy operations also suppresses the implicitly declared move constructor and move assignment, so adding `= delete` to an otherwise movable type silently makes it non-movable.
Deleting only the copy constructor leaves copy assignment usable; close both copy operations (and the move story) explicitly.
`= delete` removes the operation for members and friends too, so factories or deserialisation code must build a new object from raw values instead of duplicating the original.

variants.name: boost::noncopyable private base (library mixin)
variants.implementation_notes: The classic mixin: derive privately from `boost::noncopyable`; the base declares its copy operations private (C++03) or deleted (C++11) and keeps constructor and destructor protected so it can only be used as a base, and every derived class inherits the property. Choose it when the same guarantee must be recognisable across many classes, when the code must still compile as C++03, or when Boost is already a dependency - the old `<boost/noncopyable.hpp>` path is deprecated in favour of `<boost/core/noncopyable.hpp>`. Because the base predates move semantics it blocks moves as well, so a movable-but-not-copyable resource must delete its own copy operations instead of inheriting.
pitfalls: Use private inheritance: a public base makes 'is-a noncopyable' part of the type's interface and lets subclasses expose it.
boost::noncopyable also blocks moves, which is the wrong answer for a movable-but-not-copyable handle; delete the copy operations directly instead.
Including the same empty base twice through different paths makes it ambiguous - a hard error, not a size problem.

variants.name: CRTP non-copyable base (template mixin)
variants.idiom_name: template <class T> class NonCopyable, derived-type-typed assignment
variants.implementation_notes: The template form from More C++ Idioms parameterises the base over the derived type, so the suppressed assignment is declared against `T&` and each derived class gets its own empty base - the catalogue notes this keeps the empty-base optimization usable when such mixins are combined. It preserves the mixin's readability (the intent appears in the base-specifier list) while the compiler can report the derived type in diagnostics. Template special-member rules are easy to get wrong, so treat the shape as incomplete until proven: a `static_assert` next to the class is what actually documents and locks the guarantee.
pitfalls: The suppressed assignment names T rather than the base, so verify with `static_assert`/traits that copy assignment as well as copy construction is rejected - a template form can hide a gap.
Each derived type instantiates its own base, so there is no single `NonCopyable&` type to query or store; use the non-template base when a cross-cutting API is needed.
The declaration-only form gives access/link diagnostics instead of a deleted-function error, and empty definitions would make copies legal inside the class.
